rows.title: Asian American and Pacific Islander Women
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Critical Thinking: Think critically in reading, writing, and/or speaking about topics relating to how various aspects of identity such as race, ethnicity, class, gender, sexuality, religion, national origin, and immigration status shape AAPI women's experiences; their cultural representations, productions and practices; and social/ political activism, thereby identifying problems, theses, arguments, evidence and conclusions.

Communication: Write or speak about topics relating to how various forms of AAPI women's cultural productions and practices such as AAPI women's writings, films, music, art, creative expressions in new media, social/ political activism, and daily life activities reveal historical and contemporary issues facing AAPI women as well as their resistance to patriarchy; (neo)colonization; (cultural) imperialism, multiple oppressions of race, class, and gender; orientalism; and forces of globalization and global capitalism, thereby addressing problems, formulating theses, making arguments, analyzing and weighing evidence, and deriving conclusions.

Personal Actions and Civil Responsibility: Demonstrate an ability to understand one's role in society, take responsibility for one's own actions, make ethical decisions in complex situations, and understand that one has the power and ability to make decisions that make a difference on a personal, professional and global level.
Global Awareness: Articulate similarities and contrasts among cultures, times, and environments, demonstrating an understanding of cultural pluralism.

objectives: Analyze and articulate common Ethnic Studies concepts and terms such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, eurocentrism, white supremacy, settler colonialism, (cultural) imperialism, militarism, neocolonialism, racial and global capitalism, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, and anti-racism in analyzing AAPI women’s experiences, particularly their oppressions and resistances.

Apply theory and knowledge produced by AAPI women to describe the histories, critical events, contributions, lived-experiences, and social struggles of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in the United States, emphasizing agency and group-affirmation.
Describe the impacts of the racialized and sexualized representations of AAPI women in American popular culture and mainstream media on AAPI women.

Use the lens of AAPI feminism, anti-colonialism, anti-racism, and equity to critically analyze how the lives of AAPI women are shaped by broader structural forces in both historical and contemporary contexts.

Critically analyze how race, ethnicity, class, gender, sexuality, religion, national origin, immigration status, and other aspects of identity shape AAPI women’s experiences; their cultural representations, productions and practices; and social/ political activism.

Critically analyze various forms of AAPI women’s cultural productions and practices such as AAPI women’s writings, films, music, art, creative expressions in new media, social/ political activism, and daily life activities to investigate historical and contemporary issues facing AAPI women as well as their resistance to patriarchy; (neo)colonization; (cultural) imperialism, multiple oppressions of race, class, and gender; orientalism; and forces of globalization and global capitalism.

Critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by AAPI women are relevant to current and structural issues such as national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in reproductive health and immigration policies.
Recognize, analyze, and challenge issues of power, oppression, injustice, as well as social and economic violence against AAPI women.

Describe the impact of activism by and/or about AAPI women and actively engage with anti-racist and anti-colonial issues and the practices and movements in Asian American and Pacific Islander communities for a just and equitable society.

outcomes: Communication: Write or speak about topics in anthropology of gender and sexuality, thereby addressing problems, formulating theses, making arguments, analyzing and weighing evidence, and deriving conclusions.

Critical Thinking: Think critically in reading, writing, and/or speaking about topics in the anthropology of gender and sexuality, thereby identifying problems, theses, arguments, evidence and conclusions.
Global Awareness: Articulate the varieties of biological and cultural adaptations pertaining to gender and sexuality, and demonstrate an understanding of cultural pluralism.

objectives: Apply the general perspective, terminology, and theory of cultural anthropology to the study of gender and sexuality.
Discuss past and present anthropological research on gender in non-Western cultures including examples of current research and controversies.
Explain the important distinctions between the concepts of sex, gender, gender role, gender identity, sexuality, and sexual orientation.
Describe and explain sexual and gender diversity in Western and non-Western cultures.

Compare and contrast gender practices of diverse cultures including gender division of labor, relative status of men and women (and members of other genders, if applicable), gender and politics, gender and kinship, and gender and religion.

Evaluate various theories used to explain aspects of gender and sexuality that vary from culture to culture (e.g., gender division of labor or status of women and men), citing strengths and weaknesses of each theory.
Explain the complex relationship between human culture and human biology as applied to gender and sexuality.
Analyze current world events and issues that pertain to gender and sexuality using an anthropological perspective.
Explain how the knowledge and perspective of anthropology can further an understanding of gender and sexuality in Western society today as well as in other societies and historical periods.

rows.title: Introduction to Medical Anthropology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Civic Actions and Personal Responsibilities: Demonstrate an ability to understand one’s role in society, take responsibility for one's own actions, and make ethical decisions in complex situations.

Communication: Write or speak about topics in Medical Anthropology, a combined sub-branch of biological and cultural anthropology concerned with the application of anthropological and behavioral science theories and methods to address questions about health, illness and healing, thereby addressing problems, formulating theses, making arguments, analyzing and weighing evidence, and deriving conclusions.

Critical Thinking: Think critically in reading, writing, and/or speaking about topics in Medical Anthropology, a combined sub-branch of biological and cultural anthropology concerned with the application of anthropological and behavioral science theories and methods to address questions about health, illness and healing, thereby identifying problems, theses, arguments, evidence and conclusions.
Global Awareness: Articulate similarities and contrasts among cultures, times, and environments, demonstrating an understanding of cultural pluralism.

objectives: Define the subfield of medical anthropology within the context of the scientific discipline of Anthropology.
Examine theoretical questions of how one frames “illness,” “health,” “healing” or “medicine” as an object of anthropological understanding.
Discuss the cultural dimensions of illness and the medicalization of social problems in the United States as well as in non-Western societies.
Explore integrative approaches from different sciences used by medical anthropologists to assess the nature of health and disease.
Identify current methodologies used by medical anthropologists to study disease etiology, the experience of suffering, and the provision of health services.
Analyze issues of health, illness, and medicine over the lifecycle of an individual.
Discuss how certain health disparities come to be identified with particular stigmatized social groups, or by sex and gender.
Evaluate the relationship between food production, diet, socio-economics and health.
Define the effects of stress and emotional trauma within the context of a cultural and historical paradigm.
Explore how the inter-relationships of stress, anxiety, and adaptation are modified by the culture in which they occur.
Examine the general changes in health subsystems (epidemiology, demography, and nutrition) resulting from stages of external cultural contact and acculturation.
Distinguish the difference in meaning for health programming described as (1) cultural competent; (2) cultural sensitive; (3) cultural responsive; or (4) culturally-based.
Evaluate how cultural and social factors inform the design, delivery, and evaluation of clinical encounters, preventive services and international health programs.
Examine the field of bioethics and review the past influences of colonial and postcolonial history with regard to the introduction and dominance of biomedical research and intervention.
Differentiate how international health programs can be made culturally and socially relevant to the communities at which they are aimed.
